cards.title: Time exponents for multiple-string LCS over fixed alphabets
cards.formal: Determine the optimal deterministic polynomial-time exponent function \(\tau(\sigma,k)\) for longest common subsequence of \(k\) strings over an alphabet of size \(\sigma\), on the entire domain \(D=\{(\sigma,k)\in\mathbb N^2:\sigma\ge2,\ k\ge2\}\). For each fixed pair, let \[\tau(\sigma,k)=\inf\bigl\{c\ge0:\ \exists A\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ \forall n\ge n_0\ \forall(s_1,\ldots,s_k)\in(\{1,\ldots,\sigma\}^{\le n})^k,\ A\text{ outputs an LCS within }Cn^c\text{ operations}\bigr\},\] where \(A\) ranges over the correct uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithms defined below, and \(n,n_0\) are integers. Supply a function \(g:D\to\mathbb R\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|g(\sigma,k)-\tau(\sigma,k)|\le1/100\) for every \((\sigma,k)\in D\). This explicitly broadens the source’s proposed constant-fraction exponent improvement into determination of the underlying exponent function; it is not claimed to be equivalent to that yes/no question.
cards.why: Multiple-string alignment has a rapidly growing dependence on the number of sequences, even though it is polynomial-time solvable when that number is fixed. A small alphabet may constrain the combinatorial choices enough to change the leading exponent. Determining the full exponent function would separate the cost of coordinating many strings from the expressiveness supplied by a growing alphabet, and would sharpen the fine-grained limits behind exact sequence comparison.
cards.status_note: The 2017 source explicitly poses the fixed-alphabet exponent-saving question. This card records a transparent quantitative broadening to the underlying exponent function, not an equivalent reformulation or a claim that every parameter pair is unresolved. Bounded later-work checks through 14 September 2026 found conditional bounds and different string variants, but no unconditional determination of this entire function.

progress.text: Abboud, Backurs and Vassilevska Williams, Theorem 2, show that an exponent improvement for k-LCS with alphabet size proportional to k would refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. The alphabet dependence is part of the result.

Bringmann poses the fixed-alphabet fractional-exponent improvement in Section 4.3, Open Problem 3, printed page 120. Section 4.2 defines the common-subsequence task and asks a different time-space question.

Golan et al., CPM 2026, review the multiple-string worst-case bounds in Section 1 and obtain algorithms for a hybrid that also imposes a substring requirement. Their result does not determine the exponent function here.

sentences: Multiple-string LCS finds a longest string that occurs as a subsequence of every input.
The target is the optimal deterministic time exponent for every fixed alphabet size and fixed number of strings.
It makes the source’s question about a fractional exponent saving into an explicitly broader quantitative function.
Resolving the function would identify how alphabet size changes the computational cost of coordinating many sequences.
Acceptance requires a Lean-certified error of at most one hundredth at every parameter pair, while retaining the source question separately.

cards.definitions: A subsequence of a string \(s\) is any string obtained by deleting positions while preserving the order of the retained symbols. An LCS of \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) is a string that is a subsequence of every input and has maximum possible length. The algorithm must output one such string exactly, with arbitrary tie-breaking; inputs may have unequal lengths or be empty. The input includes an integer bound \(n\ge2\), the \(k\) lengths and all symbols, stored explicitly in a read-only array with one length or symbol per word; each length is at most \(n\). Output symbols and output length are written explicitly. For each fixed \((\sigma,k)\), the algorithm is one finite program independent of \(n\), with no nonuniform advice or tables supplied as a function of \(n\). Its word width is \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for some fixed integer \(d\ge\sigma+k+4\), allowed to depend on the program and the fixed pair. A constant number of word reads, writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, additions, subtractions, multiplications modulo \(2^W\), or unsigned divisions with quotient and remainder by a nonzero word each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(W\) returns zero. Work memory starts at zero; all input access, preprocessing, addressing and output are charged. Each local operation accesses only constantly many words, and no real arithmetic, oracle, quantum operation or random coins are allowed. Running time is worst-case over all valid tuples for the stated length bound. The constants \(C,n_0,d\) and program may depend on \(\sigma,k\), but not on \(n\) or the input strings. An admissible algorithm must be correct and terminate on every valid input, including sizes below \(n_0\). The alphabet and string count remain fixed when taking the exponent; neither is hidden as a growing function of \(n\). The infimum is finite: exact multiple-string LCS has an \(O(n^k)\) algorithm for each fixed pair, while explicitly outputting a length-\(n\) common string requires linear time. Thus \(1\le\tau(\sigma,k)\le k\). No algorithm attaining the infimum is assumed to exist.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide one unambiguous mathematical function \(g\) on all of \(D\), together with a complete correct proof checked in Lean of the pointwise absolute bound \(1/100\) in exponent units. A family of certified intervals of width at most \(1/50\) covering every pair qualifies through their midpoints. The answer may be an expression or certified evaluation rule; merely repeating the defining infimum is not a determination. Bounds on the infimum must respect its possible nonattainment: a claimed endpoint need not be achieved by one algorithm with exactly that exponent. A result only for one alphabet, one number of strings, average-case inputs, approximations, or substring variants does not meet the entire criterion. Conditional bounds alone do not give an unconditional determination. The tolerance concerns the real-valued exponent function, not an approximation to the output subsequence or a constant-factor characterization of the full running time.

context_blocks.text: Bringmann’s Open Problem 3 asks whether \(k\)-LCS has an \(O(n^{(1-\varepsilon_\Sigma)k})\) algorithm for a fixed alphabet \(\Sigma\). The surrounding paragraph contrasts this with conditional \(n^{k-o(1)}\) hardness when the alphabet can grow linearly with \(k\). Recovering this alphabet dependence is essential; the inherited title alone omitted it.

The benchmark’s permitted quantitative broadening is used here to ask for \(\tau(\sigma,k)\). The original proposed fractional saving remains a separate sourced question. In particular, approximating every exponent to \(1/100\) need not decide whether an arbitrarily small strict exponent improvement exists or whether an infimum is attained. No equivalence between those targets is asserted.

Subsequences retain order while allowing gaps. Requiring a contiguous substring, an increasing sequence, a compressed representation, or a multiplicative approximation changes the task. The unrestricted worst case also differs from parameter bounds that become fast only when the optimum is very close to the input length.

Abboud, Backurs and Vassilevska Williams give conditional exponent lower bounds when the alphabet size is allowed to depend linearly on the number of strings. Their result does not supply the same uniform exponent barrier while one alphabet is held fixed and the number of strings varies. The source also records weaker parameterized hardness for constant alphabets, which leaves room between different linear coefficients in the exponent.

Golan, Kraus, Porat and Shalom review exact multiple-string LCS in CPM 2026 and study a hybrid subsequence–substring requirement. The faster algorithm for that hybrid does not solve unrestricted multiple-string LCS. Their discussion also distinguishes exact algorithms from recent two-string approximation results.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
